title: Ask for operations with a purpose
statement: Ask only for operations with a purpose in the scenario, since an arbitrary instruction tests whether students follow directions, not the skill.
example: A Grade 3 line-plot question asked for the total number of crayons in all lengths except 2 1/2 inches, with no reason given for leaving that length out.
detail: The evaluator passed a Grade 3 line-plot question asking for the total number of crayons in all lengths except 2 1/2 inches without flagging the exclusion, and review found no reason for leaving out exactly that value. A must-fail audit was added to the math rules: a data-interpretation question must connect its operation to a real purpose in the scenario, and an arbitrary count, sum, exclusion or filter fails educational accuracy because it only tests whether a student can follow an unmotivated directive. The rule rests on that one reviewed item.

evidence.quote: Questions that ask students to perform arbitrary, unmotivated operations on data — for example, counting items that exclude a specific value without a stated reason, summing an arbitrary subset, or filtering by a criterion that is not meaningful in the scenario — fail `educational_accuracy` because they do not assess a genuine mathematical skill; they only test whether a student can follow an unmotivated directive.
The evaluator passed a Grade 3 line-plot question asking 'What is the total number of crayons in all lengths except 2 1/2 inches?' without flagging the unmotivated exclusion criterion.
A good data-interpretation question connects the operation to a real purpose in the scenario
